summary: For ages 7–9, break the intuitive category split that 'the Sun' and 'stars' are two different kinds of object, and replace it with 'the Sun is a star — our nearest one.' The decisive move is making distance concrete: a bright thing looks big and dazzling up close and shrinks to a faint dot far away, so the tiny night stars are really other Suns, unimaginably far off, sitting at wildly different huge distances rather than all stuck to the sky together. Anchor this in the Sun-centred solar-system picture (Sun at centre, all eight planets orbiting). Keep the level to 'nearest star' only: the Sun is NOT the biggest or brightest star — it appears brightest because it is closest, and apparent-vs-actual brightness ranking belongs to a later topic. Guard the sun-safety rule throughout: never look directly at the Sun.
misconceptions: The Sun is not a star / is a completely different kind of object from stars (it is a star — the nearest one)
Stars are tiny (they are enormous; they only look like points because they are extremely far away)
The Sun is the biggest or brightest star in the universe (it appears brightest only because it is the closest; many stars are far bigger/brighter — detail for a later topic)
The Sun does not move / the stars orbit the Sun the way planets do (only planets and other solar-system bodies orbit the Sun; other stars are separate suns far away)
All stars are the same distance away / are stuck to the sky (they are at wildly different, huge distances)

activities.title: Drag the Sun away until it looks like a night star
steps: Start with the familiar dazzling Sun filling the view, then use a distance control to drag it farther and farther from Earth, watching it shrink and dim until, out among the night sky, it becomes just one more tiny dot that cannot be told apart from the other stars

Reverse the process on a labelled distant star: pull it closer until it swells and blazes into a big, dazzling disc like the Sun (real stars differ in size, colour and brightness, so up close it would not be an exact copy of the Sun)
Read the caption as it updates: 'same kind of thing — a star — just nearer or farther'
Keep an eye on the small Sun-at-the-centre orbit picture in the corner (Sun at centre, all eight planets orbiting) to stay anchored in the solar system
activities.insight: The Sun is a star — our closest one — and the tiny night lights are other Suns far, far away; being so much closer is the main reason the Sun looks big and dazzling while other stars look faint and tiny. The child makes this transformation happen rather than being told it.

activities.title: A felt near-vs-far brightness comparison
steps: Look at a bright torch or lamp held close up — note how big and dazzling it appears
Watch or walk it steadily farther away and describe how it shrinks to a faint point
Connect this to the night sky: discuss how distant stars look tiny only because they are so far away, not because they are small
Use a distance line showing the Sun as the nearest star and other stars placed vastly farther — at very different, huge distances
activities.insight: Apparent size and brightness depend on distance; a bright object shrinks to a faint dot far off, which is exactly why real, enormous stars look like tiny specks at night, and the stars sit at wildly different huge distances rather than all the same distance.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal: the Sun and the night sky
steps: Tap the daytime Sun to reveal 'our nearest star'
Tap a night star to reveal 'another Sun, very far away'
Lift a flap on 'why is the Sun so big and bright?' to find 'because it's the closest star'
Say aloud or match the facts: the Sun is a star; it is the nearest star; other stars are other Suns very far away
activities.insight: Naming and reframing: the Sun is a star — the closest one — and the night stars are distant Suns.

activities.title: Explain WHY the Sun looks biggest
steps: Answer: 'What is the Sun?' (a star / a planet / a moon)
Answer: 'Why does the Sun look bigger and brighter than other stars?' choosing 'it is the closest' over the distractor 'it is the biggest'
Describe or diagram the solar system as the Sun at the centre with all eight planets orbiting around it
Respond to the two-tier prompt: 'Is the Sun a star too, or a completely different kind of object? If it IS a star, why does it look so much bigger and brighter than all the others? Tell me WHY.'
activities.insight: A child who understands the concept says the Sun is an ordinary star seen up close and explains its appearance by DISTANCE, not by the Sun being the biggest star.

checkQuestion: At night you see tiny points of light called stars. In the daytime you see the Sun. Is the Sun a star too, or a completely different kind of object? And if it IS a star, why does it look so much bigger and brighter than all the others? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: The Sun IS a star — the same kind of object as the tiny points of light we see at night. It looks so much bigger and brighter only because it is by far the CLOSEST star to Earth; the other stars are enormously farther away, so they look like tiny dots. The Sun sits at the centre of our solar system with the planets orbiting around it.
